title: Transmission patterns and future forecasting of mpox: a review of mathematical modelling approaches for prediction and public health preparedness

analysis.scope_and_question: Mpox has shifted from a disease mainly associated with zoonotic spillover in Central and West Africa to a recurrent global public-health threat involving sexual-contact networks, household transmission, international mobility, ecological persistence and clade-specific uncertainty.

The analysis highlights the role of sexual-contact networks, household transmission, international mobility, and ecological persistence in shaping mpox dynamics. Mathematical models have provided insights into mechanisms such as heavy-tailed sexual-contact distributions, behavioral adaptation, vaccination, and case isolation during the 2022 clade IIb outbreak. The implications of this work suggest that a forecasting-first approach could enhance early warning systems, targeted vaccination strategies, communication planning, and health system preparedness, especially in areas with fragmented or delayed surveillance.

title: Maternal and neonatal mpox in Nigeria: a multicentre case series highlighting diagnostic challenges, transmission pathways, and neonatal outcomes

analysis.scope_and_question: Mpox during pregnancy and the neonatal period remains insufficiently characterised, particularly in endemic African settings. We describe three mother–infant pairs managed in southern Nigeria, highlighting maternal recognition, possible transmission pathways, neonatal manifestations, and outcomes.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: We conducted a retrospective case series of three neonates with laboratory-confirmed mpox managed at three hospitals in southern Nigeria between January and May 2025. Cases were identified during routine clinical care following recognition of neonatal vesiculopustular illness and confirmation of monkeypox virus (MPXV) infection by real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) on lesion swabs. Maternal clinical histories, epidemiological information, investigations, management, and outcomes were retrospectively reviewed.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Maternal mpox was not recognised before delivery, and none of the women underwent MPXV testing. All three male neonates developed fever and disseminated vesiculopustular eruptions between days 4 and 9 of life and presented to hospital between days 14 and 16. Neonatal lesion swabs were positive for MPXV by RT-PCR (cycle threshold values, 19.70–21.60), while varicella-zoster virus PCR results were negative. Management was primarily supportive. Two neonates recovered completely. The third died at home on day 24 of life following interruption of inpatient care. No post-mortem examination was performed; therefore, the immediate cause of death could not be established. The available evidence did not permit determination of the route of neonatal infection.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Early neonatal presentation, uncertainty about transmission pathways, and challenges sustaining inpatient care highlight important gaps in the recognition and management of mpox at the maternal–newborn interface.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Improved clinical suspicion, timely molecular diagnosis, and continuity of care are important priorities in endemic settings.

analysis.summary_en: This review article presents a multicentre case series of three mother–infant pairs in southern Nigeria with laboratory-confirmed mpox. The study highlights the challenges in diagnosing maternal mpox, the uncertainty surrounding neonatal transmission pathways, and the variability in neonatal outcomes. Maternal mpox was not identified prior to delivery, and none of the women underwent MPXV testing. Neonatal cases presented with fever and disseminated vesiculopustular eruptions, with two recovering and one dying at home due to interrupted inpatient care. The study underscores the need for improved clinical suspicion, timely molecular diagnosis, and continuity of care in endemic settings. However, the lack of post-mortem examination and the inability to determine the route of neonatal infection represent significant evidence gaps.

The findings suggest that targeted training and policy interventions are essential to improve HCW readiness for Mpox outbreaks in SSA.

title: Viro-BERT: Whole-Genome Attention for Robust Viral Pathogen Classification from Next-Generation Sequencing Data.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Classifying viral pathogens from next-generation sequencing (NGS) data is central to diagnosis and genomic surveillance.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Most deep learning classifiers, however, read only a fixed window at the start of each genome, typically a few hundred to a few thousand base pairs, and so ignore more than 95% of the sequence of large DNA viruses such as monkeypox virus (MPV) and herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV-1).
analysis.methods: We refer to this problem as Truncation Blindness. Here we present Viro-BERT, which splits a complete genome into overlapping 512-token windows, encodes each window with a shared DistilBERT encoder, and averages the window-level class probabilities in a Late Fusion Consensus layer.
analysis.main_results: Viro-BERT reached 96.79% accuracy and a macro-F1 score of 96.17%. At 5% noise, the accuracy of the 1D-CNN fell by 5.57 percentage points, whereas Viro-BERT still classified 93.68% of genomes correctly.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These results indicate that whole-genome context is needed for viral classifiers that remain reliable on noisy clinical data.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that Viro-BERT can improve the reliability of viral classification in clinical settings where sequencing data may be noisy or incomplete.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report specific limitations of the study design.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces Viro-BERT, a novel deep learning model designed to classify viral pathogens from next-generation sequencing data. The research addresses the issue of Truncation Blindness, where traditional classifiers focus only on a fixed window at the start of the genome, neglecting the majority of the sequence. Viro-BERT processes overlapping windows across the entire genome, using a shared DistilBERT encoder and a Late Fusion Consensus layer to aggregate results. The model was compared with 1D-CNN, Bi-LSTM, and RoBERTa baselines on 14 viral classes, achieving 96.79% accuracy and a macro-F1 score of 96.17%. When tested with 5% random substitution noise, Viro-BERT maintained 93.68% accuracy, outperforming 1D-CNN, which dropped by 5.57 percentage points. Positional and attention analyses on HSV-1 showed that Viro-BERT utilizes diagnostic signals from across the genome rather than just the 5' end. These results highlight the importance of whole-genome context for reliable viral classification in noisy clinical data, with implications for improving diagnostic accuracy and genomic surveillance. The study is limited to abstract-only evidence, and the findings are based on a comparison with other models using the same segmentation and training protocol.
